reasons.C1: Testing leniency and reward regimes on LLM sellers is policy-relevant, but replicating a human lab game with LLMs is a familiar genre.
reasons.C2: Nothing exists yet; plan is sound with contamination test and preregistration, but 80 duopolies plus harness in 48 hours solo is uncertain.
reasons.C3: Problem, regimes, planned control and scorecard are clear; limitations are thin and no findings exist to communicate.

levers.C1: Show a regime where LLMs respond opposite to humans, with a mechanism, so the result changes how authorities design leniency for agents.
levers.C2: Deliver the laissez-faire positive control and all four regimes with intervals, passing the contamination test, before the deadline.
levers.C3: Produce the human versus LLM table with intervals plus an honest limitations section on contamination and refusal effects.

T9.verdict: Well-designed plan with the right controls, but today it is a proposal; I would score it on delivery, not intent.

reasons.C1: Secret collusion offers resemble injection attacks on agents; the trusted-partner and harmless-request conditions are a sensible, modestly novel design.
reasons.C2: Strong scaffolding with frozen preregistration and many tests, but zero real model runs, no model chosen, no results.
reasons.C3: Design is described, but report, results and demo are not seen; a reader cannot learn any finding.

levers.C1: Compare susceptibility across model families and framings, linking acceptance rates to known injection or sycophancy behaviour.
levers.C2: Run the 60 games on real models, pass the positive control, and report say-versus-do gaps with Wilson intervals.
levers.C3: Write the report with one headline figure of acceptance and pricing per condition, plus limitations and the dual-use appendix.

J3.verdict: Careful engineering of an empty experiment; until a real model runs, there is nothing to judge but the harness.

reasons.C1: Self-funded ranking on agent payment rails is a real, neglected detection problem, but wallets are not shown to be LLM agents.
reasons.C2: Honest held-out split and permutation test, yet labels share the rule's evidence; on independent features accuracy drops to 0.67, p = 0.14.
reasons.C3: Findings and limitations are present, but the 17-page report exceeds the 8-page limit and no demo was seen.

levers.C1: Establish that flagged wallets are operated by LLM agents and tie the detector to agent collusion rather than generic wash trading.
levers.C2: Obtain labels independent of the rule's features and more test families, then show held-out accuracy with a tight interval.
levers.C3: Cut to 8 pages leading with the independent-feature result and circularity caveat, plus one figure of a recovered ring.

Q5.verdict: Real data and honest statistics, but circular labels and unclear AI agency make the headline 0.82 weaker than it looks.

reasons.C1: Monitorability of non-text vector channels between models is a neglected carrier problem with clear oversight relevance, though no collusion game.
reasons.C2: Real models, reproduced checkpoints, shuffled-label controls; but countermeasures only face non-adaptive channels, channels trained pre-sprint, no significance tests.
reasons.C3: Figure 1 makes the snapping result instantly clear; the 13-page report exceeds the 8-page limit.

levers.C1: Embed the vector channel in an actual collusion task so overseers see a coordination gain that text monitors miss.
levers.C2: Train channels adaptively against snapping and quantization, and report whether the defence survives with seeds and significance tests.
levers.C3: Trim to 8 pages around Figure 1 and state plainly that the defence result holds only against non-adaptive senders.

D2.verdict: Strongest evidence in the field, but a defence tested only against non-adaptive attackers is a starting point, not a result.
